name: Marjolet
description: Marjolet is an elegant two-player card game from southwest France, and the direct ancestor of Bezique and Pinochle. Played with a 32-card French deck, it combines trick-taking with melding, featuring the unique 'Marjolet' (trump Jack) that can be melded with different Queens. The game is known for its tactical depth despite simple rules.

overview.description: Marjolet is an elegant two-player card game from southwest France, and the direct ancestor of Bezique and Pinochle. Played with a 32-card French deck, it combines trick-taking with melding, featuring the unique 'Marjolet' (trump Jack) that can be melded with different Queens. history.origins: Played in southwest France. The name 'Marjolet' refers to the trump Jack, which has special melding powers. It is the direct ancestor of Bezique and the grandparent of Pinochle.
timeline: Traditional: Played in southwest France for generations
Evolution: Expanded into Bezique (two-deck version) and eventually Pinochle
Documentation: First detailed English description by Howard Fosdick, based on French sources
Present: Remains a regional game in France; Bezique and Pinochle are more widely known internationally
history.cultural: A classic French cafe game, appreciated for its elegant balance between trick-taking and melding strategies.
history.evolution: The game expanded into Bezique by adding a second deck and more complex melds. Pinochle further evolved from Bezique, particularly in America.

setup.deck: 32-card 'French deck' - remove all cards below 7 from standard deck. Ranking: Ace (high), 10, King, Queen, Jack, 9, 8, 7. Note: 10 is second-highest, right below Ace.
setup.dealing: Deal 6 cards to each player. Turn one card up next to remaining deck (stock) to determine trump suit.

rules.objective: Win the hand by scoring the most points through melds and capturing Aces and Tens in tricks (brisques). Win the game by being first to make 500+ points across hands.
rules.gameplay: Non-dealer leads to first trick. Opponent may play any card (no obligation to follow suit). Higher card of led suit wins, or trump wins against non-trump lead. Winner of trick may declare melds, then both players draw from stock (winner draws first). Winner leads to next trick.
keyRules: Non-dealer leads to first trick; no obligation to follow suit during stock phase.
Higher card of led suit wins the trick, or any trump beats non-trump.
Winner of each trick may declare melds (e.g. marriage, Marjolet with Queen), then winner draws first from stock, opponent second.
First to 500 or more points wins the game; points from melds and from Aces and Tens (brisques) in tricks.
In the final 6 tricks, must follow suit and win if possible.

strategy.basic: Balance between playing cards to tricks and keeping cards for melds. Ideally, play low cards to tricks while keeping meldable combinations in hand. Win tricks when you need to declare melds.
strategy.intermediate: The tension between capturing Aces/Tens in tricks vs. using them in melds. Sometimes discard a high card early to develop a meld. The Marjolet (trump Jack) is extremely valuable - it can be melded multiple times with different Queens.
strategy.advanced: Memory is essential - track which cards have been played to know what melds are possible. Decide when to 'close' by drawing the last stock card based on your hand strength. In the final 6 tricks, carefully manage your cards to follow the stricter rules.
tips: Be flexible in which melds you chase - adapt based on what cards you draw
The trump Jack (Marjolet) is uniquely powerful because it can be remelded
Consider the timing of melding - showing cards gives opponent information
In the final 6 tricks, planning is crucial - you must follow suit and win if possible
The Dix (7 of trumps) is always worth 10 points - don't forget to claim it

scoring.description: Points from melds and from brisques (Aces and Tens) taken in tricks. First to 500 or more wins the game.
scoring.winCondition: First to reach 500 or more points across hands wins the game. Points come from melds declared and from Aces and Tens (brisques) captured in tricks.
